..
Saturday through Thursday: A parade of wet storm systems with 
ties to subtropical moisture will take aim at the Pac NW 
through the period. The Olympics, West Slopes of the North 
Cascades, and southwest British Columbia are favored to receive 
a brunt of the moderate to heavy precipitation as each axis of 
moisture comes in with a southwest to northeast orientation. 
Periods of light to moderate precipitation will at times extend 
into the East Slopes of the Cascades and North Idaho with 
generally light activity over Central and Eastern WA. Between 
each round of precipitation, there will be a short-lived breaks 
allowing for some drying. Ensembles are in good agreement with 
the general, active weather pattern across the Eastern Pacific 
and into the Northwest with subtle differences coming with 
exactly how much of the moderate to heavy rain will extend over 
the immediate crest and potentially fall over the Cascade burn 
scars (Little Giant, Sisi, Pioneer) creating some concern for 
debris flows. The pattern is not particularly conducive for 
heavy rain directly over these scars but each slug of moisture 
will be capable of 0.20-0.50" every 24 hours. These soils are 
becoming saturated following the 0.25-0.50 inches of rain that 
fell over these scars over the last 12-15 hours. The main 
uncertainty comes with the intensity of these rains. 

Saturday will bring the first short-lived break in the wet weather.  
Satellite reveals a deeper trough digging into the Eastern 
Pacific which will allow heights to rise over the Inland NW and 
bend the next plume of subtropical moisture south to north off 
the WA Coast. Breezy south to southeasterly winds will develop 
over the Inland NW with the air mass warming 3 to 6 Celsius at 
850 mb. Gusty winds are expected over the Blue Mountains, 
Palouse, Camas Prairie, and L-C Valley where there is a 50-70% 
chance for gusts 20-25 mph. The approaching cold front will move
into the Cascades overnight and across the Inland NW Sunday 
morning. In addition to bands of moderate rain, gusty westerly 
winds will be likely. I expect a period of winds to surface with
the cold front passage overnight and remain gusty into Sunday 
morning and early afternoon as the boundary layer becomes well 
mixed. There is 60-70% chance for wind gusts >30 mph and 10-30% 
chance for wind gusts >40 mph. Given the strong cold air 
advection (850mb temperatures cooling 6-7 Celsius), gusts of at 
least 30 mph seem like a sure bet but it may be harder to mix 
down the 40kt winds overnight from 2000 feet above ground layer.
I do have some concern that the models may be undergoing the 
mixing overnight for some of the higher benches on the 
Waterville Plateau and across the upper rim of the Columbia 
Basin and Palouse. Forecast wind gusts have been increased given
these concerns. These stronger winds to subside closer to 30kts
following the cold front passage leading to gusts closer to 30 
mph through Sunday morning.

Travelers heading over the Cascade passes will mainly encounter 
rain for Saturday and Saturday evening. Following the cold front
passage Saturday night, rain showers will change to snow 
showers for Stevens and Washington Pass. While Stevens Pass is 
not expected to receive impactful snow, will need to closely 
monitor where the Puget Sound Convergence Zone sets up which 
could lead to local accumulations of 1-2 inches. NBM is 
forecasting 3-4 inches for Washington Pass. Otherwise, 
precipitation with the front Saturday night into Sunday morning 
will deliver another 0.25-0.50" across the upper river valleys 
of the East Slopes and aforementioned burn scars and upwards of 
0.70-1.00" to the immediate crest. Rainfall amounts in Idaho and
eastern WA will vary from a few hundreths to quarter of an inch
along the Montana border with little to no rainfall in the 
Cascade rain shadow. The highest intensity rain for the Cascades
will come right along the cold front overnight. 

Monday-Tuesday: The pattern is a bit messy with weaker waves 
coming through the region but with an usually moist air mass 
remaining overhead. This will continue to bring on and off 
preciptiation, generally light and lower impact on Monday but 
rain intensities will increase on Tuesday as more developed warm
front develops. This will bring the next chance for another 
0.10 to 0.50 to the Cascades and tenth to quarter of an inch 
over Eastern WA and North Idaho. 

Wednesday-Saturday: There is moderate confidence for another 
ridge to blossom over the region Wednesday into Friday 
delivering the next period of dry conditions. Given several days
if on and off rain, its almost a guarantee there will be areas 
of fog and low stratus. Uncertainty increases late Friday into 
Saturday whether the next front pushes inland or remains off the
coast with high pressure in control. By this time, confidence 
is lower that the front will have ties to the richer moisture 
and is expected to weaken with lighter rainfall amounts. /s
